stt: Ask HN: What literature do you read?
x:
East of Eden is my favorite book I've read in the last several years. Beautiful end to end and very moral. If you've read it it's totally worth reading Journal of a Novel: a collection of letters Steinbeck wrote to his editor every day as he was writing East of Eden. It's a fascinating window into the mind of a master deliberately creating a masterpiece.

Other favorites: Crossing to Safety by Wallace Stegner, In Our Time by Hemingway, The Magus by John Fowles, 100 years of solitude, Moby Dick (perhaps a precursor to all modern fantasy?) Stranger in a Strange Land, and Infinite Jest. I've also loved both of DFW's big essay collections: Consider the Lobster and A Supposedly Fun Thing I'll never Do Again.

stt: Ask HN: Great fiction books that have had a positive impact on your life?
x:
In highschool, John Fowles' The Magus [1.] really hit me: its twisting plot and content really opened up the world of fiction and writing for me. Great departure from the typical books in highschool English/Literature classes.

William Gibson's Neuromancer [2.] was excellent in providing an escape from reality, very engrossing, and fascinatingly prescient of the some societal trends extrapolated into the future.

1. The Magus - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magus_(novel)

2. Neuromancer - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuromancer

stt: Ask HN: What book had a big impact on you as a child or teenager?
x:
It was the books in my Dad's library that first got me to read for pleasure.  I remember him suggesting The Lord of the Rings but it would be several years before I read it. 50 years later I can't actually remember what I read first but over the course of my late childhood, the one that sticks out the most is:

The Magus by John Fowles

I was maybe 14 at the time. You just never know because kids are weird.
